hints: Recall the general products when a Group 2 nitrate is heated strongly, think metal oxide plus two gaseous products.
Check atom balance for Ca, N and O, then assign (s) for solids and (g) for gases.
walkthrough:
Recall what Group 2 nitrates give on heating**
All Group 2 nitrates decompose in the same way on strong heating. You keep the metal as a solid metal oxide, and the nitrate part breaks up to give nitrogen dioxide gas and oxygen gas. So for calcium you already know the three products are $\mathrm{CaO}$, $\mathrm{NO_2}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$.

Balance and add state symbols**
Start from $\mathrm{Ca(NO_3)_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{NO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}$. You need 2 N on the right, so put 2 in front of $\mathrm{NO_2}$. Then recount O: left has 6 O, right has $1 + 4 + 2 = 7$ O. Doubling everything clears the odd oxygen: $$2\mathrm{Ca(NO_3)_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CaO} + 4\mathrm{NO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}$$ Anhydrous $\mathrm{Ca(NO_3)_2}$ and $\mathrm{CaO}$ are solids, so (s), while $\mathrm{NO_2}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$ are gases, so (g).

hints: Think about the colour of the gaseous nitrogen-containing product formed in this decomposition.
Think about the colour of the starting calcium nitrate solid and the solid oxide left behind.
walkthrough:
Picture the gas coming off**
$\mathrm{NO_2}$ is very distinctive. It is a brown, pungent gas, sometimes seen as brown fumes in the test-tube. Oxygen is colourless so you do not see it separately. The brown colour is your key test for nitrate decomposition.

Picture the solid left behind**
Both anhydrous $\mathrm{Ca(NO_3)_2}$ and the product $\mathrm{CaO}$ are white solids. So you see a white solid remaining in the tube, with no charring or other colour change, while the brown gas escapes.

Final answer: Brown gas / brown fumes of $\mathrm{NO_2}$ evolved.
White solid / white residue of $\mathrm{CaO}$ remains.

hints: Recall whether $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ or $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$ is more soluble to state the trend down Group 2.
Write the enthalpy cycle link: $\Delta H_{sol} = -\Delta H_{latt} + \Delta H_{hyd}$ and consider what happens to both terms as cation size increases.
Compare how much $\Delta H_{latt}$ changes versus $\Delta H_{hyd}$ when the cation gets larger but the large $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ anion stays the same.
Link a less exothermic $\Delta H_{sol}$ to lower solubility.
walkthrough:
State the observed trend clearly**
Going down from $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ to $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$, solubility falls sharply. Magnesium sulfate is very soluble, calcium sulfate is sparingly soluble, and barium sulfate is essentially insoluble. That is the pattern you describe first.

Set up the energy balance for dissolving**
Dissolving can be thought of in two steps: break the lattice apart (endothermic, equal to $-\Delta H_{latt}$) then hydrate the gaseous ions (exothermic, $\Delta H_{hyd}$). So: $$\Delta H_{sol} = -\Delta H_{latt} + \Delta H_{hyd}$$ The more exothermic $\Delta H_{sol}$, the more soluble the salt tends to be.

See why both enthalpies get less exothermic**
Down the group $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ba^{2+}}$, the cation gets larger so charge density falls. A smaller, more highly charging ion attracts both lattice anions and water molecules more strongly. So both lattice breaking costs less and hydration releases less energy. In other words, both $\Delta H_{latt}$ (as a negative value for formation) and $\Delta H_{hyd}$ become less negative.

Explain why the balance shifts against dissolving**
Here the anion $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ is very large. Changing the cation size has only a relatively small effect on the lattice energy because the interionic distance is already dominated by the big sulfate. Hydration, however, depends strongly on the cation alone, so $\Delta H_{hyd}$ falls off much more quickly. The loss in hydration energy outweighs the saving in lattice breaking, so $\Delta H_{sol}$ becomes less exothermic, even endothermic, and solubility decreases.

Final answer: Solubility of Group 2 sulfates decreases down the group.
Both $\Delta H_{latt}$ and $\Delta H_{hyd}$ become less exothermic / less negative down the group as cationic radius increases.
$\Delta H_{latt}$ becomes less exothermic to a smaller extent than $\Delta H_{hyd}$ because the large $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ dominates the lattice.
Therefore $\Delta H_{sol}$ becomes less exothermic / more endothermic down the group, so dissolving is less favoured.
